title: Looking for some film recommendations where monotony serves a broader thematic purpose

commenti.body:
The Turin Horse is such a great example. 

Possibly the best example I can think of is [Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975)](https://letterboxd.com/film/jeanne-dielman-23-quai-du-commerce-1080-bruxelles/)
[removed]

I think Malick's *A Hidden Life* is a perfect example for the morbid side of monotony. I wrote a bit about it when the film first came out. (I think the film is on Disney+)

https://a-a-birdsall.medium.com/morbid-monotony-a-hidden-life-terrence-malick-2019-f8c484ee57eb
Jeanne Dielman for sure. The film practically hypnotizes you until the smallest variation becomes shocking.

[Solaris has a ~5 minute scene of riding down the highway, contrasting the natural beauty of the preceding sequence.](https://youtu.be/rswYl7RLRNE?si=qf88YZ4eBZs8WBDH) I think people rag on it, but I've always found it weirdly hypnotic.

What you're referring to is called "Slow Cinema".  Here's the wiki link and it has a whole bunch of great examples to check out.

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow\_cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_cinema)
Also the nine minute candle scene at the end of *Nostalghia.* Tarkovsky was a genius at making monotony utterly captivating.

I'd recommend Jim Henson's film The Cube (if you don't have depression and anxiety maybe seeing the protagonist through that lens could help - this movie is the embodiment of the quote "hell is other people"; it's an experimental film where a man finds himself stuck in a cube). There's a filmed version of the Play True West on YouTube with Gary Sinese (lieutenant dan) and John Malkovich - you're in for doozy, especially if you've ever had a sibling rivalry. Sunset Limited, written by Cormac McCarthy, is a great play style film of two men, Samuel Jackson and Tommy Lee Jones, as a man of faith and a man of faithlessness discussing among other things what Albert Camus considered the fundamental question of existence - should I commit suicide? One of my favorite films, which is best going in without spoiling the twist, is the Iranian film the Taste of Cherry - It's about a suicidal man looking for someone to bury him after he kills himself. It's a divisive film. Another user here with suicidal depression was very underwhelmed. The twist, if you see this film, I compare it to the reverse of the entrance to Oz. 

Another filmmaker that many would consider too monotonous is Robert Bresson. He directed unprofessional actors to not act. His style is like moving mosaics. Minimal camera movement  and not too flashy editing or music. Mouchette, Balthazar, and The Devil Probably are my favorite perhaps because I could relate to characters the most; if you've seen this films you might be concerned with what that says about me if you knew me; but suffice it to say I'm doing alright on medication and in therapy.
Would you look at that, a tailor-made watchlist. Cheers.
[removed]

I thought OP meant monotony as a theme, not monotony as in lengthy shots with no action or dialogue. I think the scenes you mention are profound and contemplative, not monotonous. 

I'm thinking of Nuri Bilge Ceylan's "Distant", where one protagonist comes up against the monotonous nature of the world when he tries to advance his life, and the other one is mired in monotony, practically paralyzed in it, because his wife left him.
The OP's first example The Turin Horse is on that list.
I agree that The Turin Horse is about the monotony of living (crushing monotony in its case). Not all slow cinema has monotony as a theme.
[removed]

I haven't actually seen it yet but from what I've read about it, it sounds like *Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles* is a pretty famous example of what you're looking for. It immerses you in the minute rhythms and actions of a woman's daily routine for over 3 hrs.

I think The Zone of Interest which is currently in theatres, fits what you’re looking for. It’s a little difficult to talk about without spoiling the whole thing, though. 

A Ghost Story also might fit – there’s a brilliant 10 minute long scene in which Rooney Mara eats a pie, but otherwise the film is about Humans’ relationship with time.

Thought it was pretty cool to see 1970s Moscow for awhile. That scene and the ending are the only things that have really stuck with me in the years since I’ve watched that movie. Brilliant movie too btw

I dont think ‘monotony’ is fair terminology. I like the term ‘andante’ for more slower paced and methodical cinema. It can have a very meditative and hypnotic affect.

Anything by Apichatpong Weerasethakul is great at this sort of masterful pacing.

Gus Van Sants death trilogy, last days, Gerry and Elephant.

Paris Texas maybe fits the bill here? 

All the works of Nuri Bilge Ceylan.

Drive my car is another masterpiece of pacing. Everything is savoured.
[removed]
[removed]
Jeanne Dielman came to mind too! Based on descriptions I've come across it seems like it fits the bill, though I haven't seen it myself. What did you think of it?

*Days* by Tsai Ming-Liang seems like most obvious example of his and by extension his filmography is mottled with cinematic protraction of lived moments, but I guess I wouldn’t say they all deal with monotony, it’s more of a immersive way in which Tsai communicates human existence

Thanks for the link! I think examples of "slow cinema" are really interesting here. There is a good deal of overlap between some of the movies I have in mind and a handful of the movies included in the Wiki you shared. But as /u/RSGK mentions, there are some important differences between monotony as a theme versus monotony within a shot. 

Your *Stalker* example is actually great for this; there are shots that are hypnotic and slow, with very little happening (e.g., the trolley car ride into the Zone), but I don't see a broader pattern of monotony in the film that serves a thematic purpose.
This is exactly right, and thanks for the rec! I've never heard of that film before, excited to add this to the watchlist.

Oh that's interesting, this film didn't come to mind even though it might be my favorite Malick movie. It's been a bit since I've seen it, but what makes you think of this movie as monotonous? Looking forward to giving your blog post a read.

Nice! Zone of Interest has been on my watch list since I first heard about it. What did you think of it? 

I loved *A Ghost Story*, including Rooney Mara's dedication in that scene haha. I can think of a few scenes (pie scene notwithstanding) that are very slow and methodical. I would probably put it more in the "slow cinema" category but am open to why you might think otherwise.

I loved it. 

Similar to the other person who responded by saying, "practically hypnotizes." I was fully hypnotized....the mundane routine over and over pulled me more into the movie and just as the other response said, it made small variations, shocking. I don't want to spoil any scene so I'll just say that some simple, meaningless, day-to-day thing that is just a few minutes off and I wouldn't bat an eye at, instead I could feel her stress or unease.

For sure, I think there is a good deal of overlap between "slow cinema" (or andante as you mention) and the kind of films I have in mind. And I think homing in on how monotony is used picks out a particular kind of "slow cinema" film. Lot's of overlap in that Venn diagram. 

Your recs are spot on for the kind of meditative and hypnotic effect you mention, though I haven't seen any of Van Sant's death trilogy so I'll check it out!

The only specific motif I remember is the postman coming every day without news. Other than that, it was mostly just the overwhelming sense of days going by and nothing changing for good or for bad, through which this incredible sense of dread was conveyed, like I couldn't bear to watch any longer in a way that resembled, but was not nearly fully explained by, boredom. Which sounds like a criticism since we are so averse to boredom, but it isn't.

I hope that makes sense, if you didn't feel it when you watched yourself, it's a very complicated emotion for me to try to explain lol.

Awesome, thanks for all these recs. I've haven't seen *The Cube*, but that sounds really intriguing. 

Though I loved *A Taste of Cherry* (*Sunset Limited* less so, though Tommy Lee Jones and Samuel L. Jackson are both great), it didn't strike me as a particularly monotonous movie. What made you feel that way about it?
Ahh ok, I just need to sit down and watch it. I think I've been intimidated by the runtime and knowing it's supposed to be repetitive, but it sounds like the payoff is worth it.

Of those three Elephant is his finest in my opinion so maybe start with that and if you enjoy move onto the others. Paranoid park too maybe. Lots of cool slow/meditative bits in that.

Columbus (2017) is a film I keep recommending as well to people who like things at a slower pace. I don’t think that film gets talked about enough.

Jones' character seemed to be in a state of ennui, like from his depressed perspective everything is just dull and grey and monotonous. So while the film isn't monotonous, I think his character thinks existence is crushing monotony. It's like Sylvia Plath's depression of seeing the world through a bell jar.

Police, Adjective focuses on the monotony and bureaucracy of police work in a really fantastic way, especially in its thematic connection to the ineffectiveness of the work. Highly recommended, one of my favourite movies.
[removed]
Audition by Takeshita Miike purposefully goes really slow at the start to lull you into a serene state, maybe even boredom. It makes the second, utterly terrifying half hit way harder
Came here to suggest The Seventh Continent, saw your list, surprised it's not on there.
That scene is filmed in Japan isn't it? The street signs seem to be in Japanese
[removed]
[removed]

Bleak Moments (1971) uses monotony to convey the despair and social isolation of the protagonist, as she works and also cares for her mentally challenged sister.

Clockwatchers (1997) - it's been a while since I watched it, but I can still remember the buzzing overhead lights in that dreary office.

I have HEARD (ie, read critical assesments) that this is an aspect of EYES WIDE SHUT.

This is also a deliberate aspect of the original DAWN OF THE DEAD ("boredom at mall life - getting all you want)

The 1975 film “ Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du commerce, 1080 Bruxelles” is to me exactly the type of film you are thinking g about.  There is intense monotony of domestic routine. Tables are set, food is prepared, beds are made laundry is washed, and it all plays out in nearly real time. The film has an 3+ hour run time. And there are twists. Lost and lots of twists.
These both seem exactly what I was looking for, added them to the watchlist. Thanks!
This sounds perfect, thanks for the rec!
Definitely, I think that captures the character's outlook very well.

The Brown Bunny does it better than any movie I’ve seen and that includes Jeanne Dielman and Tarkovsky. Just ruminating in solitude and misery until the gut punch of the finale. Absolutely brilliant movie.

Perfect, thanks!

And couldn't agree more, Columbus is one of my favorites of the of the past couple 5-6 years.

Haha I feel that, trying to convey a specific emotional response to a film is such a pain. I really liked your write-up of A Hidden Life, by the way. It makes me want to revisit it; it's been way too long since I've seen it.

There was a 1996 movie I still think about called Chronicle of a Disappearance. There was no real story to it. The filmmaker was an American Palestinian returning to visit his family in the West Bank and Israel, and he shows different vignettes of people going about their daily life. It’s also quite funny; one segment has the filmmaker standing around in pajamas and fuzzy slippers while Israeli soldiers in riot gear search his apartment. By the end you realize that the “disappearance “ in the film’s title is Palestinian identity.
[removed]

Probably Haneke's *The Seventh Continent*. Normally, people talk about *Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles*, *The Seventh Continent* and *Turin Horse* (in increasing order of nihilism) together. The first two acts serve to emphasize the monotony in the life of a couple of middle-class Austrians. Haneke also shoots some of the scenes in a POV sort of manner, as if cluing us into their lives (Haneke likes holding a mirror up to the audience in his films, I've noticed), which makes the third act all the more tragic.

Kaurismäki's *The Match Factory Girl* plays out in the same way as  *Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles* and has a monotonous but entrancing opening sequence
Nice, another Porumboiu! If it's anything like *12:08 East of Bucharest*, I'll probably love it...
[removed]

The most monotonous movie ever made has to be Andy Warhol’s [Empire](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_(1965_film)), 8 hours of a single shot. I had the chance to see a screening of the 6 hour version in college.

I think, a film that would definitely fit in this categorie ist Charlie Kaufmann's "I'm Thinking of Ending Things" (2020). The monotony of two protagonists sitting in a car extends over the entire film.

Friends who saw the movie with me said it was difficult to endure the monotony. But when it disappears and the movie turns to surrealism, you miss it. And when the monotony returns, you're a little happier and look forward to it.   
Furthermore, towards the end of the movie the realities become blurred and at least I thought nostalgically of the monotony of the road trip at that moment.

I think this is beautiful.

Steve McQueen, maybe? 

Thematically, he focuses on people trying to impose their own agency on rigid, uncaring systems. While none of his films use *repetition*, I’m fascinated by his use of time. Short, shocking moments are explored in granular detail before melting off into an endless expanse of boredom.

Hunger would be my pick, though Shame and 12 Years A Slave also do it.
I enjoyed buffalo 66 but never gave brown bunny a chance. Is there multiple versions? Or was the controversy that the version show at cannes was never released and much improved upon?

Geyrhalter's documentaries are all about monotony, but without characters : *Our Daily Bread*, for instance...

James Benning also makes documentaries that are the pinacle of monotony : *Ten Skies* (clouds); or *13 Lakes* (landscapes); or *RR* (Trains)...

Peter Hutton, again monotonous documentaries. E.g. *At Sea*. On board a tanker...

Sokurov's *Spiritual voices*, another long haul documentary about soldiers monotonous lives waiting for something to happen on the border.

Maybe Wang Bing's *Tiexi Qu West of the Tracks*, a documentary on the daily lives of factory workers while their factory is being dismentled.

Fiction wise, and still in the realm of Contemplative Cinema:

Roy Andersson paints a stylised reality but is all about monotony: *Songs from the Second Floor*... as a starter.

Tsai Ming Liang, perhaps is most monotonous film is *What Time is It There?* about time passing slowly away from the loved one.

Sharunas Bartas made his most monotonous film in *Freedom*.
I love that sequence. Tarkovsky chills me out.

Melancholia (2011) uses it to a certain extent. Also The Lobster (2015).

I also think a lot of Irish (or Irish-set) stories have moments of tranquil monotony, perhaps to do with the weather/isolation & their tradition of stoicism & poetry? I'm thinking of The Banshees of Inisherin off the top of my head.

& David Lynch frequently uses it, the most obvious example I can think of is the 'sweeping' scene in The Return. Or The Straight Story (1999).

Ha! This is probably the best example you could have given. Didn't even think about Warhol's films. But I guess Empire and Sleep are at the top of the list for monotony as a theme. I'm curious, what was it like watching Empire for 6 hours? I've never had a film experience like that.
Oh, The Seventh Continent is a great example. Didn't think of that one. And thanks for the rec, sounds exactly what I'm looking for. The Match Factory Girl is now on the watchlist.
These are all great, thanks! Haven't watched a documentary in a while so I'll check these out.

These sound great, thanks! I have seen Roy Andersson's *You, the Living* (2007), and didn't like it very much but *Songs from the Second Floor* sounds like it's worth a watch and a good reason to revisit Andersson's work.    

On the other hand, I loved *Goodbye Dragon Inn* (2003) but that's the only film I've seen from Tsai Ming Liang. Looking forward to checking out *What Time is it There?*
Thanks for the rec, really excited to check this one out.

Roy Andersson's films are all lookalike (except his debut) so chances are you might find it exactly like the first one you saw. I'm not saying his films are redundant and not worth seeing, each film has a story to tell.

A lot of Tsai's films are like that. *The Hole* is also quite monotonous.
Since you mentionned *Into Great Silence*, I thought documentaries were OK to be mentionned too.

Goodbye Dragon Inn, Stray Dogs, or honestly anything by Ming-liang Tsai (except maybe his feature debut, Rebels of the Neon God)

ooh and the newly released vietnamese film, Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell (2023), saw this on a festival last month and it was one of the most meditative cinematic experience i've ever had

I'll butt in and say personally I don't think they are worth watching for their full runtime. There are more museum pieces that you walk into a dark room, sit and watch for as long as you want and leave. 

If you want to watch a Warhol movie like this, I'd suggest Vinyl (1965). It's an "adaption" of A Clockwork Orange. Interestingly Kubrick, perhaps in a nod to this movie, uses the same technique (slow zoom into a closeup of the main character) as Warhol to open the film.
I was more enraptured by this scene than with the climax of any major action /superhero/whatever film in the last decade plus.
Yeah, docs are definitely fair game. In fact, you could argue that documentaries are particularly well-suited for these kind of themes.

There are a couple of Japanese films from this year where monotony is used to great effect:

*Evil Does Not Exist* contains numerous long monotonous scenes without much action or progression as a way of drawing you into the environment, have a conservationist theme.

*Perfect Days* provides the main character, Hirayama, with a monotonous and tedious daily routine, so that any slight (or not-so-slight) variation becomes personally fulfilling.

Synecdoche, New York came to mind here as well.  Philip Seymour Hoffman continues to endlessly, circle back on his life, once it starts going sideways, with increasing baroqueness.  I'm Thinking of Ending Things definitely deserves a rewatch...good call.

Clockwatchers is great, and preceded the very anticorporate submotif of the late '90's (Fight Club, The Matrix, Office Space, American Beauty) by a couple years.  Parker Posey, Lisa Kudrow, and Toni Collette are all in peak Indiewave mode and it's delightful.   Definitely worth a revisit.

That makes sense, and that was my exposure to *Sleep*. Saw it as a museum piece and watched for a couple of minutes before moving on. And thanks for the rec, hadn't heard about Vinyl before.
